source_row.rationale: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm can present with acute abdominal or back pain and shock or hypotension, making Option D the single best answer. Distal embolization and thrombosis are recognized vascular complications but do not best explain this abrupt pain-plus-hemodynamic-collapse pattern. Enlargement without rupture can cause pain but does not best account for sudden hypotension.
source_row.source_detail: StatPearls Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm — History and Physical: enlarging AAA can cause abdominal, flank, or back pain; ruptured AAA may present dramatically with shock and abdominal pain. Suspected rupture is a vascular emergency. Current StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm entry; clinical content live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, endocrine/vascular emergencies and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm develops sudden severe abdominal and back pain with hypotension. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
